The Reformation principle that Scripture alone is the final norm of doctrine.
Calvin's doctrine, building on Augustine, that God eternally elects some to salvation.
The Catholic Reformation council (1545-63) responding to the Reformers.
The 21st ecumenical council (1962-65) which renewed Catholic teaching on liturgy, ecclesiology, and ecumenism.
The movement seeking visible unity among separated Christian churches.
The sociological claim that modernity inevitably reduces religion's social significance.
Nietzsche's image, in The Gay Science section 125, for the collapse of belief in the Christian God in Western culture.
Feuerbach's view that God is humanity's projected ideal self.
Freud's term for religion in The Future of an Illusion: wish-fulfilment rooted in childhood need.
The early-2000s movement of Dawkins, Dennett, Harris and Hitchens emphasising scientific naturalism.
Jurgen Habermas's diagnosis of contemporary society as one in which religion has returned to public life.
Kant's supreme moral principle: act only on that maxim which you can will to be a universal law.
A command of reason that applies conditionally, based on a desired end, contrasted by Kant with the categorical.
For Kant, the only thing good without qualification; a will that acts from duty, not inclination.
Bentham's view that each individual action should maximise pleasure and minimise pain.
Mill's refinement: we should follow rules whose general observance maximises happiness.
Bentham's method for measuring pleasure using factors such as intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity, fecundity, purity, and extent.
The branch of ethics concerned with the meaning and status of moral language and judgments, rather than first-order moral questions.
The view that moral properties are reducible to natural properties; 'good' can be defined in non-moral terms.
G.E. Moore's charge that defining 'good' in terms of any natural property commits a logical error.
Moore's view that 'good' is a simple, non-natural, indefinable property known by intuition.
A.J. Ayer and Stevenson's view that moral statements express emotions and seek to influence others; the 'boo/hurrah' theory.
R.M. Hare's view that moral statements are universalisable prescriptions, not mere expressions of feeling.
Aristotle's term for human flourishing or 'living well', the final end of all human action.
Excellence or virtue, the quality by which a thing fulfils its function (ergon).
Aristotle's view that moral virtue lies between extremes of excess and deficiency, e.g. courage between rashness and cowardice.
Practical wisdom, the intellectual virtue of deliberating well about how to act in particular circumstances.
Alasdair MacIntyre's 1981 work which diagnosed modern moral discourse as fragmented and called for a return to Aristotelian virtue.
Aristotle's argument that the good for humans is the activity of the soul in accordance with reason and virtue.
God's rational ordering of all creation; the divine wisdom directing every action and movement.
The participation of rational creatures in the eternal law, knowable by reason.
The law revealed through Scripture, supplementing natural law where reason is insufficient.
Particular legal codes derived by reason from the natural law to govern communities.
The first principle of practical reason: 'good is to be done and pursued, and evil avoided'.
The fundamental goods that natural law directs us to: preserve life, reproduce, educate offspring, live in society, and worship God.
The theory developed by Germain Grisez and John Finnis, identifying basic goods grasped by practical reason without grounding them in human nature.
Finnis' seven irreducible goods: life, knowledge, play, aesthetic experience, sociability, practical reasonableness, and religion.
John Paul II's 1993 encyclical reaffirming traditional moral absolutes against proportionalism.
The method of applying moral principles to particular cases, developed especially by Jesuit moral theologians.
Hume's challenge that one cannot derive an 'ought' from an 'is'; raised against natural law's use of nature.
The view that moral norms vary by culture; a modern challenge to natural law's claim of universal access through reason.
An action genuinely aligned with the natural law and human flourishing.
An action that appears desirable but, on rational analysis, is contrary to natural law.
The intention or motive of an action, central to its moral evaluation.
The outward action itself, evaluated together with intention.
A principle permitting an action with both good and bad effects, provided the bad effect is foreseen but unintended.
A 20th-century Catholic revision (e.g. Bernard Hoose) allowing 'proportionate reasons' to override traditional moral absolutes.

philosophy-of-religion-ancient-philosoph.d: Philosophy of Religion: Ancient Philosophical Influences (Plato, Aristotle)
terms: Aristotle explained things through material, formal, efficient and final causes, with the final cause - purpose or telos - completing the explanation.
Plato and Aristotle on the soul
Plato saw the soul as immortal and separable from the body, while Aristotle treated the soul as the form of the body, not normally separable.
Plato held that beyond the changing world of appearances lie eternal, perfect Forms, which reason alone can know.
Plato's image of prisoners mistaking shadows for reality, picturing the philosopher's ascent from illusion to knowledge of the Forms.
The highest Form, which Plato likened to the sun: it gives reality to the other Forms and makes knowledge of them possible.
Aristotle's eternal, unchanging being that moves the universe as a final cause, attracting motion like an object of desire while thinking only of itself.

philosophy-of-religion-arguments-based-o.d: Philosophy of Religion: Arguments based on Observation & Reason
terms: Observation-based arguments yield at best probable conclusions, while the reason-based ontological argument claims necessity but rests on definition.
Aquinas's first three Ways argue from motion, causation and contingency that there must be a necessary, uncaused being - God.
Gaunilo parodied Anselm with a perfect island, and Kant argued that existence is not a predicate that adds to a concept.
Hume attacked the design analogy as weak, suggested alternative explanations, and argued the evidence cannot establish the God of classical theism.
Anselm argued from reason alone that 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived' must exist in reality as well as in the mind.
Aquinas's fifth Way and Paley's watch argue from order, regularity and purpose in nature to an intelligent designer; arguments from observation.

philosophy-of-religion-religious-experie.d: Philosophy of Religion: Religious Experience, Problem of Evil
terms: Evil as privation of good entering a perfect creation through the Fall, so that God is not the author of evil.
Sceptics offer physiological and psychological explanations and argue private experiences cannot be verified as evidence for God.
An Irenaean approach: God made immature creatures at an epistemic distance, and a challenging world enables free growth towards perfection.
The challenge that evil and suffering count against an all-powerful, all-loving God: logically (Mackie) or evidentially (from evil's sheer extent).
Visions, voices, conversion and mystical experiences, whether individual like Paul's conversion or corporate like the Toronto Blessing.
James marked mystical experiences as ineffable, noetic, transient and passive, and judged them by their practical fruits rather than their causes.

religion-ethics-applied-ethics-euthanasi.d: Religion & Ethics: Applied Ethics (Euthanasia, Business Ethics, Sexual Ethics)
terms: The debate over whether businesses have duties beyond profit: Friedman's shareholder view against stakeholder theories of wider responsibility.
Debates distinguish voluntary from non-voluntary euthanasia and active killing from withdrawing treatment, alongside arguments about assisted dying.
The sanctity view holds life is sacred and God-given, while quality-of-life views measure the value of life by wellbeing and autonomy.
Premarital and extramarital sex, contraception and homosexuality are assessed through natural law, situation ethics, Kantian and utilitarian approaches.
Natural law appeals to the preservation of life and double effect, while situation ethics asks what agape love requires in each situation.
Business ethics asks when exposing wrongdoing is justified and whether good ethics is ultimately good business.
Conscience is reason at work: synderesis grasps first moral principles and conscientia applies them to actions, so conscience can err through ignorance.
Ayer's non-cognitivist view that moral statements express feelings of approval or disapproval - 'boo/hurrah' - and are neither true nor false.
Conscience is the super-ego: internalised parental and social disapproval producing guilt, a psychological rather than divine faculty.
Moore argued 'good' is a simple, indefinable property known by intuition, and accused naturalists of the naturalistic fallacy.
The study of the meaning and status of moral language - what 'good' means and whether moral claims can be true - rather than which acts are right.
The cognitivist view that moral statements describe natural facts about the world, for example identifying goodness with pleasure or flourishing.

religion-ethics-normative-ethical-theori.d: Religion & Ethics: Normative Ethical Theories (Natural Law, Situation Ethics, Kantian, Utilitarianism)
terms: Introduction to the Principles of Morals; greatest happiness for greatest number; hedonic calculus measures pleasures by 7 criteria.
Hard to predict consequences; ignores justice (gang rape majority); demands too much; comparing utilities.
Bentham's 7 factors: intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity, fecundity, purity, extent; calculates utility.
Utilitarianism 1863; qualitative distinction; better Socrates dissatisfied than fool satisfied; rejected pure hedonism.
Developed by R.M. Hare and popularised by Peter Singer; maximise satisfaction of preferences, not pleasure; Singer's basis for animal liberation and the drowning child analogy.
Mill's refinement: follow rules that maximise utility; avoids problematic act-utility e.g. lying not always wrong.
The pre-Fall state in which reason rightly governed will and passions.
Adam's primal disobedience, transmitted to all his descendants.
The disordered desire that remains as a wound even after baptism.
The 'lump of damnation' from which God elects some to salvation.
Disordered love that turns from God to creatures as ends in themselves.
Rightly ordered love which refers all created goods to God.
The conviction that the gospel demands a particular concern for the poor and oppressed.
Right action; liberation theology emphasises orthopraxis alongside orthodoxy.
Small grassroots Catholic groups practising Bible study and social analysis.
Freire's term, central to liberation theology, for the process of becoming critically aware of social structures.
Social system of male dominance critiqued by feminist theology.
Mary Daly's term for the inherited masculine language about God; she sought its radical critique.
Grace preached as forgiveness without repentance, communion without confession, baptism without discipleship.
Grace that calls us to follow Christ, costing a man his life, but giving him true life.
The German Protestant movement opposing Nazi co-opting of the Church; Bonhoeffer was a leader.
Bonhoeffer's prison-cell vision of a Christianity stripped of metaphysical religion for a 'world come of age'.
German for 'vicarious representative action'; central to Bonhoeffer's Ethics.
Plato's metaphysics: eternal, immaterial paradigms in which sensible things participate.
The highest Form in Plato's Republic, which gives intelligibility to other Forms.
Plato's Republic Book VII image: prisoners mistake shadows for reality until the philosopher escapes to the sun.
Aristotle's material, formal, efficient, and final causes.
Aristotle's Unmoved Mover in Metaphysics Lambda: a final cause that moves by being the object of love.
End or purpose; the final cause of a thing.
The claim that omnipotence, omnibenevolence, and the existence of evil are logically inconsistent.
Rowe's argument that gratuitous suffering is strong evidence against theism.
Plantinga's response: God could not create free agents who always choose rightly without contradiction.
Evil as privation of good, originating in the misuse of angelic and human free will.
Hick's soul-making theodicy: a world with hardship is necessary for moral and spiritual growth.
Otto's category for the experience of the holy as mysterium tremendum et fascinans.
Based on experience; cosmological and teleological arguments are a posteriori.
Independent of experience; the ontological argument is a priori.
Aquinas's five demonstrations of God's existence in Summa Theologiae I, Q.2, a.3.
Aquinas's Fifth Way: things without intelligence act for ends, so an intelligent director exists.
Paley's argument that the intricate purposiveness of organisms implies a designer.
Kant's Critique of Pure Reason objection to the ontological argument.
The view (Freeman) that businesses have duties to all affected parties, not just shareholders.
Milton Friedman's view that the social responsibility of business is to increase its profits within the rules.
Disclosure by employees of wrongdoing; sometimes ethically required despite loyalty considerations.
Aquinas's innate disposition to grasp 'do good, avoid evil'.
Aquinas's application of synderesis to particular acts.
Freud's psychic agency that internalises parental and social prohibitions; his account of conscience.
For Kant, the only thing good without qualification.
An unconditional command of reason; the moral law in formulation.
A maxim's capacity, without contradiction, to be willed as universal law.
The highest good: virtue conjoined with happiness; Kant's postulate of God and immortality follows.
Bentham's foundation: maximise pleasure and minimise pain.
Mill's qualitative distinction protecting utilitarianism from the 'doctrine of swine' charge.
The rational participation in eternal law that human beings can discern by reason.
Self-preservation, reproduction, education, society, worship of God.
Aquinas's distinction between what truly perfects human nature and what merely seems.
An act with foreseen bad effects may be permissible if the act itself is good, the bad effect is unintended, the good does not flow from the bad, and there is proportionate reason.
Self-giving love; the only intrinsic good for Fletcher.
For Aquinas, the application of moral knowledge to particular acts; for Fletcher, the loving response in situation.
Used in the same sense in two contexts.
An attribute applies properly to one being and derivatively to another.
An attribute applies to each being in proportion to the kind of being it is.
For Tillich, a sign that participates in the reality to which it points.
Wittgenstein's rule-governed linguistic practice embedded in a form of life.
James's category with four marks: ineffability, noetic quality, transiency, passivity.
The mark of mystical experience that resists adequate verbal description.
The mark that mystical experience yields a sense of knowledge or insight.
Otto's phrase for the holy as overwhelming mystery that both terrifies and attracts.
Swinburne's rule: things probably are as they seem unless we have reason to doubt.
Swinburne's rule: we should believe others' reports unless we have reason to doubt.
A statement is meaningful only if analytic or empirically verifiable.
Requires that some observations be relevant.
A genuine assertion must rule out some possible state of affairs.
Hick's claim that religious statements are in principle verifiable after death.
Hume's posthumous 1779 work in which Cleanthes, Demea, and Philo debate the design argument.
Hume's objection that the universe is too unlike a machine to justify inference to a single, infinite designer.
Hume's revival of the idea that order could arise from chance arrangements of matter over infinite time.
Hume's distinction between relations of ideas (a priori, necessary) and matters of fact (a posteriori, contingent).
Hume's analysis of causation as merely the regular succession of events, not a necessary connection.
The 1948 BBC radio debate in which Bertrand Russell argued that the universe is 'just there' and needs no further cause.
An attempt to justify the goodness of God in the face of the existence of evil; the term was coined by Leibniz in 1710.
Mackie's formulation of the problem: God's omnipotence, omnibenevolence, and the existence of evil cannot all be true together.
The view that evil is a privation of good (privatio boni), entering creation through the free-will Fall of angels and humans.
The view that humans are created immature and grow through suffering into the likeness of God; developed by John Hick as 'soul-making'.
Plantinga's argument that a world with free creatures who sometimes choose evil is more valuable than a world of determined goodness.
The ancient challenge: if God is willing but unable, He is impotent; if able but unwilling, malevolent; if both, why is there evil?
An a posteriori argument that infers God's existence from the existence and contingency of the universe.
An a posteriori argument from the apparent design or purpose in nature to a designer, classically presented by William Paley.
An a priori argument from the concept of God as the greatest conceivable being to His necessary existence, originating with Anselm.
Knowledge or argument independent of sensory experience, derived from reason alone.
Knowledge or argument derived from sensory experience of the world.
A being whose non-existence is impossible; in classical theism, God is the only necessary being.
Augustine's view that evil is not a substance but a privation of good, a falling-away from being.
The claim that moral evil is the price of genuine free creatures who can love.
The doctrine that humanity inherits guilt and corrupted nature from Adam, transmitted by generation.
Augustine's notion that all humanity was 'in Adam' at the Fall and therefore shares his guilt.
'Happy fault'; the Easter Vigil's celebration of the Fall as occasioning the greater good of Christ's redemption.
A modern logical defence (1974) showing it is possible that even an omnipotent God could not create free creatures who never sin.
Irenaeus' view that humans are made first in the 'image' of God and must grow into the 'likeness' through moral struggle.
John Hick's term for the developmental process by which souls become virtuous through engagement with evil and suffering.
Hick's idea that a degree of separation from direct knowledge of God is necessary for genuine freedom and faith.
Hick's view that the soul-making process will eventually be completed for all persons, perhaps beyond death.
The claim that present sufferings can only be justified in the light of a final consummation.
The phrase Hick borrows from John Keats' 1819 letter, in which life is 'a vale of soul-making'.
The ancient dilemma: if God is willing but unable, He is impotent; if able but unwilling, malevolent; if both, whence evil?
Mackie's claim that the existence of any evil is logically incompatible with an omnipotent and wholly good God.
William Rowe's claim that the kinds and quantities of evil we observe make God's existence improbable.
Mackie's set of three propositions: God is omnipotent, God is wholly good, and evil exists; he argues all three cannot be true together.
Suffering caused by the free choices of moral agents.
Suffering caused by natural processes such as earthquakes, disease, and animal predation.
The logical positivist criterion that a statement is meaningful only if analytic or empirically verifiable.
A statement is meaningful only if it can be conclusively verified in experience.
Ayer's softened version: a statement is meaningful if some observation is relevant to its truth or falsity.
Flew's view that for a statement to be a genuine assertion, the speaker must concede what would count against it.
The 1950-51 'Theology and Falsification' exchange in the Oxford journal University between Antony Flew, R.M. Hare, and Basil Mitchell.
Flew's charge that theistic statements are progressively qualified until they say nothing.
Language used in exactly the same sense in two contexts; Aquinas denies our terms for God are merely univocal.
Language used in entirely different senses; Aquinas denies our terms for God are merely equivocal.
Aquinas' use of analogy where the primary instance (God) is the source of the perfection in creatures (e.g. 'God is good' as cause of all goodness).
Aquinas' use of analogy where a property is predicated proportionately to the nature of each being (e.g. divine goodness proportionate to divine nature).
For Tillich, a sign that participates in the reality to which it points; religious symbols 'open up levels of reality otherwise closed'.
Rudolf Bultmann's project of reinterpreting the mythological language of the New Testament in existentialist categories.
Wittgenstein's early Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (1921), in which meaningful language pictures facts and the religious lies 'beyond' speech.
Wittgenstein's later work, published posthumously in 1953, replacing the picture theory with the doctrine that meaning is use.
Wittgenstein's term for a rule-governed practice in which words derive meaning from their role in a form of life.
The wider context of human activity within which language games are played.
Welsh philosopher who applied Wittgenstein's later thought to religion, arguing that prayer, worship, and 'God' make sense within the religious form of life.
The view that religious truth claims are not about extra-linguistic facts but are internal to the religious community's practice.
Only one thing is intrinsically good, namely love; nothing else at all.
The ruling norm of Christian decision is love; nothing else.
Love and justice are the same, for justice is love distributed, nothing else.
Love wills the neighbour's good, whether we like him or not.
Only the end justifies the means; nothing else.
Love's decisions are made situationally, not prescriptively.
John A.T. Robinson's 1963 bestselling book advocating a 'new morality' close in spirit to Fletcher's Situation Ethics.
Anglican Bishop of Woolwich (1919-1983) whose Honest to God endorsed an ethics of love in the new theological climate.
Scottish New Testament scholar (1907-1978) who critiqued Situation Ethics, arguing love needs the guidance of rules.
The 1960s phrase for context-sensitive Christian ethics, popularised by Robinson and Fletcher.
Magisterial responses (e.g. Veritatis Splendor 1993) reaffirming moral absolutes against situationism.
The traditional principle that human life is sacred and inviolable; often invoked against situationist conclusions.
Joseph Fletcher's 1966 moral theory in which the only intrinsic good is agape love, applied freshly to each situation.
The Greek New Testament word for unconditional, self-giving love; for Fletcher, the sole moral absolute.
An approach to ethics that rigidly applies prefabricated rules without regard to context.
The rejection of all moral rules and principles, leaving each act unguided.
Fletcher's first working principle: a proposed course of action must actually work.
Fletcher's second working principle: rules are relative to the demand of love in each situation.
The Christian doctrine that God is one substance (ousia) in three persons (hypostases): Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
The doctrine that the eternal Son of God became fully human in Jesus Christ without ceasing to be divine.
'Of one substance'; the term used at Nicaea (325) to affirm that the Son shares the same divine substance as the Father.
The Chalcedonian definition (451) that Christ is one person in two natures, divine and human, 'without confusion or change'.
The Latin clause 'and from the Son', added to the Nicene Creed in the West to affirm the Spirit's procession from both Father and Son.
The mutual indwelling or 'dance' of the three persons of the Trinity, expressing their unity in distinction.
The historical process by which religion loses social significance, institutional authority, and personal plausibility.
The separation of social institutions (law, education, medicine) from religious control, a key driver of secularisation.
Bruce's term for the shift from small community life to large-scale impersonal society, undermining the social plausibility of religion.
Max Weber's term for the disenchantment of the world through bureaucratic and scientific reason.
Bruce's 2002 book defending the secularisation thesis against rational-choice critics.
Stark and Finke's rival view that religious supply rather than demand determines religious vitality.
The reconciliation of humanity to God achieved through the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
An early model (e.g. Origen, Gregory of Nyssa) in which Christ's death is the price paid to liberate humanity from the devil's power.
Anselm's account in Cur Deus Homo (1098), in which Christ's death satisfies the infinite debt of honour owed to God by human sin.
Peter Abelard's view that Christ's death moves humanity to repentant love by demonstrating God's love.
The Reformation view that Christ bore the legal punishment for human sin in our place.
Gustaf Aulen's 1931 retrieval of the patristic view that the cross is Christ's victory over sin, death, and the devil.
